title: False-Positive Bounds for Randomized Linear-Approximation Detection
summary: Nontrivial detections can be false positives without near-exhaustive queries, though they imply high correlation; rigorous false-positive and sample-complexity bounds remain open.

formal_statement.body: For an unkeyed oracle $E$, randomized detection samples inputs $x$ from $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and solves a linear system for a candidate $(\alpha,\beta,c)$. A non-trivial solution does not by itself certify a perfect linear approximation unless $E$ is queried on almost all inputs; however, any resulting false positive would imply a linear approximation with high absolute correlation. The unresolved problem is to derive rigorous bounds on the false-positive probability and on the sample complexity required by this randomized linear-system procedure, parameterized by the number or fraction of queried inputs and by the desired confidence and correlation guarantees.

scope.domain: Automated linear cryptanalysis of an unkeyed oracle using randomized linear-system detection of perfect linear approximations.
parameters: n: dimension of the binary input space
Number or fraction of queried inputs: query and sampling budget
Desired confidence: target reliability of the detection result
Desired correlation guarantee: target absolute correlation associated with false positives
scope.unresolved_remainder: Derive rigorous false-positive probability and sample-complexity bounds as functions of the query budget and desired confidence and correlation guarantees.

citations.label: On Perfect Linear Approximations and Differentials over Two-Round SPNs

progress.summary: The source observes that a linear-system solution need not certify a perfect linear approximation without querying almost all inputs, while any false positive would have high absolute correlation. It leaves false-positive behavior unanalyzed.
citation_labels: Christof Beierle et al., On Perfect Linear Approximations and Differentials over Two-Round SPNs
